messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Señor García had always been a skilled and dedicated welder. At 70 years old, he still took pride in his work, but recent events had made it increasingly difficult for him to focus on the task at hand. His wife’s passing had left an emptiness that no amount of labor could fill, and now, the memories of his time spent in captivity seemed to be closing in around him. Señor García was a victim of torture, though he rarely spoke about the experience. The trauma had been so intense that it felt as if the memories were still unfolding rather than being firmly locked in the past. Whenever he recalled the events, he would feel an overwhelming sense of rage and frustration, which often left him unable to continue his story. He had come to believe that the memory of the gunshot noise and the feeling of entrapment triggered a flood of emotions he could not control. The memories were so vivid that even simple sounds or situations at work could bring them back with startling clarity. One day, while working on a project, a sudden loud noise from another area of the workshop made him freeze in place. The sound was similar to gunfire, and it immediately transported Señor García back to those terrifying moments. He detached himself from his surroundings, almost as if he were watching someone else relive the trauma. Afterward, he would try hard not to think about what had happened, often becoming overly compliant with his coworkers in an attempt to avoid further discomfort. This cycle of triggers and maladaptive strategies was both exhausting and isolating. Señor García was certain that the event could happen again at any moment; he felt a constant fear of harm from those around him. He also harbored intense feelings of guilt for not having done more to stop what happened, which only fueled his self-blame. These negative appraisals often led to further detachment and an increased fawn response when he sensed potential threats. The weight of these thoughts made it increasingly difficult for Señor García to maintain his daily routine. His coworkers noticed a change in his demeanor; he was less engaged and more withdrawn, which affected the quality of his work. The guilt and fear were so consuming that they became self-perpetuating triggers. He would avoid certain areas or situations at work where he might encounter similar sounds or environments reminiscent of his torture. The memory itself seemed to feed into this cycle as well. When Señor García tried to recall what had happened, the details would come back in fragments, making it hard for him to explain clearly. This inability to articulate his experience left him feeling isolated and misunderstood by those around him. What finally brought Señor García to seek help was a combination of these factors. The constant triggers, his maladaptive strategies, and the overwhelming negative appraisals had taken their toll on both his work performance and his sense of self-worth. He was most afraid that he would never be able to break free from this cycle of fear and guilt. However, he also harbored a glimmer of hope—that through therapy, he might find a way to reconcile these painful memories and regain some control over his life.
